segments.t: Back in Paris, Arlette rejects the flowers and Mathias tries again to protect Jonathan's role. Their argument becomes a dispute about money, loyalty and power within the agency. Camille interrupts with the beginning of another idea. Hear the French first and follow the competing reasons.
Arlette, je veux vous parler de Jonathan Joubert.
C'est le fauteuil de Jean Gabin.
Marie-Sophie ne veut pas de tes fleurs.
Tu ne peux rien faire contre la maladie de Ryan.
On va perdre beaucoup d'argent!
Tout ne tourne pas autour de l'argent.
Arlette, votre part dans cette agence est très petite.
Et Samuel n'est plus là pour vous protéger.
Tes menaces ne m'impressionnent pas.
Je ne parle pas d'argent, je parle de dignité et de loyauté.
Marie-Sophie vaut mille fois cet idiot de Jonathan Joubert!
Alors, ton Ryan, couic!
Excusez-moi, il faut penser aux vrais fans de la série.
Oui, Camille?
Andréa voulait vous montrer quelque chose, mais pas maintenant.
Je vais revenir plus tard.
Mathias asks Arlette to reconsider the decision about Jonathan. Their conversation soon turns from the actor to the agency itself.
Arlette, je veux vous parler de Jonathan Joubert.

'Arlette, I want to talk to you about Jonathan Joubert.' Mathias uses the polite word for you to address Arlette. In this exchange she answers him with the familiar form, so the two speakers do not use the same register.
C'est le fauteuil de Jean Gabin.
'That's Jean Gabin's armchair.' The connecting word of marks whose armchair it is. French places that word before the full name, where English can attach a possessive ending.
Marie-Sophie ne veut pas de tes fleurs.
'Marie-Sophie doesn't want your flowers.' Arlette uses the familiar form of your, although Mathias addresses her politely. The possessive is plural because the flowers are plural.
Tu ne peux rien faire contre la maladie de Ryan.
'You can't do anything against Ryan's illness.' The word for nothing follows can, while do stays in its basic form. Together the negative means that no useful action is possible.
On va perdre beaucoup d'argent!
'We're going to lose a lot of money!' The quantity a lot is followed by of before money. A form of go announces the financial loss he expects if the character is removed.
Tout ne tourne pas autour de l'argent.
'Not everything revolves around money.' The negative does not mean nothing matters. It limits everything: money is not the centre of every consideration.
Arlette, votre part dans cette agence est très petite.
'Arlette, your share in this agency is very small.' The possessive your is polite, but his message is threatening. Small takes its feminine ending to match the word for share.
Et Samuel n'est plus là pour vous protéger.
'And Samuel is no longer here to protect you.' The negative expression means no longer. The following action protect stays in its basic form after the connecting word for.
Tes menaces ne m'impressionnent pas.
'Your threats don't impress me.' The familiar possessive your goes with the plural threats. The little word for me stands before the action about impressing someone.
Je ne parle pas d'argent, je parle de dignité et de loyauté.

'I'm not talking about money, I'm talking about dignity and loyalty.' The same pattern about speaking of something appears twice. Repeating it places money on one side and dignity and loyalty on the other.
Marie-Sophie vaut mille fois cet idiot de Jonathan Joubert!
'Marie-Sophie is worth a thousand of that idiot Jonathan Joubert!' The action means is worth, not costs. A thousand times makes the comparison deliberately extreme, showing her loyalty to the writer.
Alors, ton Ryan, couic!
'So as for your Ryan, that's the end of him!' The final sound imitates a brief choked cry. In this context it signals an abrupt end for the character she wants written out.
Excusez-moi, il faut penser aux vrais fans de la série.

'Excuse me, we have to think of the real fans of the series.' The impersonal expression means it is necessary. The word for to combines with the plural article before the real fans she wants them to consider.
Oui, Camille?
'Yes, Camille?' A simple yes followed by a name gives someone the floor. It can invite them to continue without agreeing to any proposal yet.
Andréa voulait vous montrer quelque chose, mais pas maintenant.

'Andréa wanted to show you something, but not now.' The past form of want reports an earlier intention. Something is an indefinite expression: Camille does not need to name the object she might show him.
Je vais revenir plus tard.

'I'll come back later.' A form of go introduces the promise to return. The final phrase means later, literally more late, rather than never coming back. Now let's listen to the whole confrontation again.
Arlette, je veux vous parler de Jonathan Joubert.
C'est le fauteuil de Jean Gabin.
Marie-Sophie ne veut pas de tes fleurs.
Tu ne peux rien faire contre la maladie de Ryan.
On va perdre beaucoup d'argent!
Tout ne tourne pas autour de l'argent.
Arlette, votre part dans cette agence est très petite.
Et Samuel n'est plus là pour vous protéger.
Tes menaces ne m'impressionnent pas.
Je ne parle pas d'argent, je parle de dignité et de loyauté.
Marie-Sophie vaut mille fois cet idiot de Jonathan Joubert!
Alors, ton Ryan, couic!
Excusez-moi, il faut penser aux vrais fans de la série.
Oui, Camille?
Andréa voulait vous montrer quelque chose, mais pas maintenant.
Je vais revenir plus tard.

Arlette refuses to sacrifice loyalty for money. Camille has not yet explained her plan, but she wants the fans to have a say. Listen again for no longer, nothing and not everything: three different kinds of negative meaning. See you next time.
Bonne soirée!
